title: The credential check is the injection point, and SQL file-write shadows an importable module instead of a web shell
index_line: T-0023 · EXEC · pre-auth SQL in the token lookup, then OUTFILE writes a module onto the interpreter's import path · c/perl/python · corroborated
invariant_violated: Two separate assumptions. First: a bearer token is treated as an opaque identifier, so the query that looks it up is written as string concatenation — the one code path where nobody expects user syntax is the authentication fast path. Second: an SQL file-write primitive is assumed to need a web-executable directory; it does not, it needs a directory the *interpreter* reads code from.

mechanism.does: a request reaches a public endpoint backed by a native handler that parses the Authorization header before any auth decision
the header value is copied into a fixed buffer verbatim, so it becomes a token string in the process image
the token is concatenated into the query that resolves the token to a user, so the injection is evaluated as part of the authentication lookup
the database parser executes attacker SQL before any credential has been validated — pre-authentication
the database account can write files (`INTO OUTFILE` available to a privileged DB user), so the query writes an attacker-authored module into a directory the interpreter searches
an unauthenticated CGI/endpoint imports that module name, the shadowing file wins over the real package, and the interpreter executes it
the import runs in the server process, giving command execution under that service account

source.http.header.value: the Authorization / bearer token header — the credential itself is the payload, so the endpoint is unauthenticated by definition

sink.sql.concat.value: the token→user lookup query (get_user_by_token-shaped), the last place anyone looks for SQLi

sink.file.write.value: SQL file-write (`INTO OUTFILE`/`DUMPFILE`), available when the DB account is privileged — the DB is a file-write gadget

fs.path.join.value: the *interpreter's import path*: site-packages, a script's directory, `.pth`/`PYTHONPATH` entries, Perl `@INC` — pick a writable one rather than a webroot

delegate.tool.value: the secondary interpreter invoked by a CGI/handler that imports the shadowed library — the execution delegate, not the SQL sink

preconditions.expr: a public endpoint's handler runs before authentication and reads a credential header
that value reaches a query by concatenation rather than a bound parameter
the DB account can write files (INTO OUTFILE requires FILE privilege and secure_file_priv permitting the target directory)

check.spec: mysql -e 'SELECT @@secure_file_priv, CURRENT_USER();' 2>/dev/null; mysql -e 'SHOW GRANTS FOR CURRENT_USER();' 2>/dev/null | grep -i FILE  # read-only privilege probe: secure_file_priv + FILE grant; do not write during a precondition check

preconditions.expr: a directory on the interpreter's search path is writable by the DB/service account, and a CGI/handler imports a shadowable module

check.spec: python3 -c 'import sys;[print(p) for p in sys.path]'; perl -e 'print join("\n",@INC)'; # cross-check against writability of each entry by the DB user

success: a quote in the Authorization header produces a SQL error / different response with no session — pre-auth, no credential needed
the written file appears in an interpreter path directory, not a webroot, and its import triggers execution on the next request to the importing endpoint
the effect is code execution with the *service* account, reachable without authentication
failure_like: the token is bound as a parameter, or looked up through a non-SQL store (LDAP, shared memory) — nothing to inject
the DB account is least-privilege (`FILE` not granted, `secure_file_priv` set) — the injection stays a read primitive
no writable directory on the import path
false_positive: an auth error for a bad token — the endpoint rejects everything without proving the token reached SQL; use a payload that only changes timing or error text, never one that could be a valid token
a file written into a webroot that the web server does not execute (or that is not reachable) — not the end of the chain
a module shadow that is never imported by anything the attacker can reach

hazards: appliance firmware means the sink is a native handler in a binary
`INTO OUTFILE` constraints vary (FILE privilege, secure_file_priv, NO_BACKSLASH_ESCAPES); enumerate them before planning the write
the import-shadow step needs the shadowed name to be imported *after* the write and by a process the attacker can invoke
non_transfers: parameterised token lookups (the whole record collapses)
unprivileged DB accounts and locked-down secure_file_priv
interpreter deployments with a read-only site-packages and no writable sys.path entry
